summary: Armanas Povilionis works at Alithea Bio on immuno-oncology and immunopeptidomics, providing agentic automation to clients. He identifies a key gap: adding more tools to agents is insufficient for collaborative scientific work, which requires a verifiable chain of receipts proving every step, ensuring trust, repeatability, and collaboration at scale. He uses a kitchen analogy—agents with more tools are like cooks with better knives, improving local efficiency, but science is like running a Michelin-star restaurant depending on external suppliers, quality produce, and consistent delivery. His vision is that as agent workflow automation matures, organizations will give agents budgets to discover services, request data, negotiate terms, and pay for work across organizational boundaries—agents becoming executive chefs rather than line cooks. Froglet is the open-source protocol built for this: agents discover, transact with, and receive verifiable receipts from external data and service providers. It sits between moving parts, integrating with payment rails, agent harnesses, execution environments, and transport protocols without requiring every node to run the same software stack—only the same interface. A single Froglet node can assume multiple roles (provider, requester, marketplace) simultaneously. Node creation generates a key pair for identity and signing; all artifacts are signed in a chain valid only if no data points are tampered with. Providers publish services to marketplaces; requesters query marketplaces, then communicate directly with providers with no third party. The demo covers remote trial usage via try.froglet.com.dev with a 15-minute temporary token, local Docker installation, and Claude integration via MCP where Claude publishes a service from a template, discovers and invokes it locally, returning the correct result of 12 for 7+5. In his conclusion, Armanas emphasizes that verifiable receipts of receipts—proving what happened—enable collaborative science and perpetual science automation, inviting the audience to join via Froglet, Alithea Bio, and GitHub.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Adding more tools to agents is insufficient for collaborative scientific work; verifiable receipts proving every step are needed for trust and repeatability at scale.
Froglet is an open-source protocol reducing named services, data-backed services, and open-ended compute to one signed flow: Descriptor to Offer to Quote to Deal to Receipt.
A single Froglet node can simultaneously assume multiple roles—provider, requester, and marketplace—using the same software with different configurations.
Every Froglet node generates a key pair on creation; all artifacts are signed in a chain that is valid only if no data points have been tampered with.
Communication between requester and provider is direct with no third party after marketplace-based discovery; quote, deal, execution, and receipt happen in one interaction.
Froglet integrates with MCP and OpenClaw/NemoClaw as a single tool, designed so an LLM drives usage rather than humans navigating complex interfaces.
Exposing a shareable service on Froglet costs a few thousand tokens and takes minutes, versus bespoke enterprise projects that can take years and cost millions.
Verifiable receipts of what happened enable collaborative science and perpetual science automation across organizational boundaries.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Armanas introduces himself and Alithea Bio's focus on immuno-oncology and immunopeptidomics. He states that adding more tools to agents is insufficient for collaborative life sciences work, which requires a verifiable chain of receipts proving every step for trust, repeatability, and collaboration at scale.

sections.title: Kitchen Analogy and Agent Budget Vision
sections.summary: Uses a kitchen analogy: agents with more tools are like cooks with better knives—local efficiency improves but science requires external suppliers and consistent delivery like a Michelin-star restaurant. Envisions organizations giving agents budgets to discover services, negotiate terms, and pay across organizational boundaries, making agents executive chefs rather than line cooks. Introduces Froglet as an open-source protocol for this vision.

sections.title: Froglet Design Philosophy and Website Overview
sections.summary: Explains Froglet sits between moving parts, integrating with payment rails, agent harnesses, execution environments, and transport protocols without requiring uniform software stacks—only the same interface. Describes node roles (provider, requester, marketplace), key-pair generation for identity and signing, tamper-evident signed chains, marketplace-based discovery, and direct peer-to-peer communication after discovery.

sections.title: Remote and Local Demo
sections.summary: Demonstrates remote trial at try.froglet.com.dev with a 15-minute token, accessing an addition provider, submitting 7+5, polling for completion, and receiving 12. Then installs Froglet locally via Docker, showing two nodes with the same ID acting as both provider and consumer simultaneously.

sections.title: Claude MCP Integration Demo and Conclusion
sections.summary: Shows Claude with Froglet MCP enabled, instructing it to check node health, publish an addition service from template, discover and invoke it locally with 5+7, and return the result 12. Notes Froglet can connect to databases or GPUs for various workloads, packaging underlying protocols without stuffing the LLM context. Concludes by emphasizing that verifiable receipts of receipts enable collaborative science and perpetual science automation, inviting participation via Froglet, Alithea Bio, and GitHub.

demonstrations: Remote Froglet trial at try.froglet.com.dev: created a 15-minute temporary token, accessed a provider token for an addition service, submitted payload with schema, provider, and input (7+5), received deal ID, polled for completion, and got result 12.

Local Froglet installation via 'HBS Froglet Dev Agent' command on Docker; confirmed two Froglets running with same node ID assuming provider and consumer roles simultaneously on same ports and IP addresses.

Claude desktop with Froglet MCP enabled: instructed Claude to check node health, publish a service from template (add two numbers), discover and invoke it locally with inputs 5 and 7, and return the result; Claude executed all steps and returned 12.
limitations: Demo used only a trivial addition service (7+5=12), not representative of complex scientific workloads
Remote trial node is small and execution time depends on load
Protocol requires all participants to use the same interface even if not the same software stack
quantitativeClaims: Exposing a shareable service on Froglet costs a few thousand tokens and takes minutes
Bespoke enterprise collaboration projects can take years and cost millions
